utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in this courtroom and those assisting us outside for the continuation of the Pre-Trial Conference which is held today and in the case, Madam Registrar, you will now call.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-PT.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that's the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic. I would like to have the appearances. Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I am Dermot Groome, I am here today with Peter McCloskey, Roeland Bos, and Ms. Janet Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic with Radovan Djurdjevic today for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I see that Mr. Mladic is present as well. This is, as I just said, the continuation of the Pre-Trial Conference which started on the 24th of April of this year, during which the Chamber considered it advisable to continue the conference to allow for additional time to resolve certain disclosure issues before the start of the trial. Over the past week, the parties have provided both formal and informal updates to the Chamber on these matters. Yesterday, an additional Rule 65 ter meeting was held with the parties for the purpose of further discussion of these matters. I'll therefore deal with disclosure and I'll start with disclosure under Rule 66(A)(ii). On the 25th of April, the Prosecution notified the Chamber and the Defence that it had discovered that due to an error in the upload on the 11th of November, the 11th of November major disclosure batch number 5, that a large percentage of Rule 66(A)(ii) material had not been in fact disclosed either on EDS or on the hard disk provided to the Defence. On the 27th of April, pursuant to the Chamber's instruction at the Pre-Trial Conference, the Prosecution updated the Defence and the Chamber with further information on the problem. This update was formalised in the Prosecution's eighth report on pre-trial preparations which was filed on the 1st of May and was discussed with the parties at yesterday's Rule 65 ter meeting. Based on those discussions, the Chamber will briefly summarise the current status of the Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosure. On the 27th of April, the Prosecution disclosed all ICTY transcripts for the 23 witnesses it intends to call before the summer break, organised in separate witness folders on a hard disk. I add to that that much of this material had already been disclosed, but we know now for sure that now all ICTY transcripts have been disclosed, therefore major parts have been redisclosed and organised in the way I described, that is, in separate witness folders which may assist the Defence in further preparation. Second, the Prosecution disclosed the B/C/S audio of the prior testimony of these 23 witnesses also on hard disk, which would allow the accused to hear portions of it. Three, the Prosecution disclosed 33 B/C/S translations of the 48 documents that had not yet been translated and will disclose the remaining translations as they are received from CLSS. And finally, number four, the Prosecution has undertaken to redisclose the ICTY transcript materials for the remainder of its witnesses by no later than the 29th of June, 2012. Mr. Lukic, in relation to that first item, that is, the transcripts which were disclosed in the separate witness folders for the first 23 witnesses, yesterday you told us that you had verified for 14 out of these 23, that they were all there apart from one, which we then together were able to find although it was not disclosed apparently. Can you now confirm that you received on the 27th of April in this disclosure batch number 15(D) also the ICTY transcripts in relation to those last nine witnesses you had not verified yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can confirm that we received all the transcripts in English for those 23 witnesses, and audios we haven't -- we didn't have time to check, but we can assume that everything is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But if you allow me, I will address it later on in more detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine as far as I'm concerned. If during verification of the audio material which was disclosed, if you find that anything is missing, don't hesitate to immediately communicate that, of course first of all to the Prosecution but also to the Chamber. Because you may have noticed that we are trying to follow the process of disclosure very closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Groome, as was discussed at the Rule 65 ter meeting, if the Prosecution and the Defence determine that the redisclosure of Rule 66(A)(ii) materials for the witnesses appearing after the summer break should occur in batches rather than all of them in one flow, the Chamber instructs the Prosecution to file a notification as each batch is disclosed. And of course the Chamber leaves it to the Prosecution and the Defence to decide whether staggered disclosure of these materials is, in fact, preferable and whether this is the manner in which you wish to proceed. Should you decide to proceed in this way, the Chamber would like to be kept informed. We want to know exactly what's happening even without having access to the content of disclosed material.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I have dealt with Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosure. If there's any matter you would like to raise in this context, Mr. Lukic, I think it would be best to do it now because otherwise it would move to Rule 68 disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if you just give me a few minutes I will express our position on this issue. So now it's obvious that we received those materials only on the 27th of April, 2012, and it's also obvious that we didn't have those materials previously, although we were raising the issue as of November last year that something is missing. It is only natural that we can start working as of 27th of April, 2012, on those missing documents and our position is that it infringes the right of the Defence if the trial would start in May 2012. The Prosecution confirmed that due to unknown problem those documents were not disclosed to us in November 2011. We accept that. We know that they are under huge pressure and that they have a lot of work to do and they were understaffed at that time. After having them employed much more staff, they were able to finalise the disclosure, but the lack of disclosed documents is not fault of Mr. Mladic, is not fault of his Defence. So we -- our position is that we shouldn't suffer because of this fault disclosure. And we think that it would be prejudice to the Defence to start trial in May, since it's not only to have documents disclosed, but we have to study them, read everything, and prepare for cross-examination of every single witness, which we are not able to do in such a short period of time. The purpose of Rule 66(A)(ii) is to enable the Defence to confront witness with all their prior statements and transcripts. The provision is of fundamental importance to the accused's right to a fair trial. It is an essential element of Rule 66(A)(ii) that disclosures occur within a specific time-limit, so as to provide adequate time and resources for the accused to examine the material and prepare its case. We know that in Karadzic case, Chamber ordered that the Prosecution not to be allowed to call any witness affected by late disclosure for a period of approximately 90 days to give the Defence time to prepare. That is actually the continuance we asked for all the time, to have at least 90 days from the disclosure until the beginning of the testimony of any witness the Prosecution intends to call. Your Honours know that we have been complaining about the lack of these materials some times now and we only received them last Friday. The Defence has lost five months of effective preparation as a result. So we reiterate our request to have the start of the witness testimonies for 90 days. That's all I have on this issue for now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I do understand that you thus repeated and further underlined and perhaps gave additional reasons for what you requested already in your filing of the 10th of April. That's how the Chamber will consider it. Thank you for this oral submission. Mr. Groome, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just briefly, Your Honour. The Prosecution accepts that there was a serious flaw in the disclosure of some of these transcripts, and I apologise to the Chamber for the issue that it's presented and for the hardship that it has caused Mr. Mladic. We offer no excuse. We gave a full explanation yesterday of the origin of that error. I would, however, point out that the majority of the material that has been the subject of this consists of public transcripts that were readily available on the ICTY web site. In effect, the amount of material that has been inaccessible to the Mladic Defence has been the private session portions of that testimony. With respect to the request for a delay of the proceedings, the Prosecution is ready to open its case on the 16th and to call its first witness on the 29th. It does defer to the Chamber on matters with respect to scheduling and whether those dates are still consistent with the fair trial rights of Mr. Mladic. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Mr. Lukic, this matter always had our full attention. We'll continue to consider it, and whether or not this will result in any change in the start of the trial is again discussed, again reviewed on the basis of your submissions today, and you'll hear the outcome of those discussions. And of course we try to resolve matters as quickly as possible so that the parties know well in advance how we are proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Only, if I may, it's not only transcripts at issue, also other documents, not only transcripts. All documents were included in this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps Mr. Groome was not in every respect correct when he said it was only transcripts, and I think you may not have been in every respect correct when you said all this material was missing. It's not all --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not all, but at least half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, at least -- of course, the Chamber is fully aware of the details of what was not disclosed and what portion that is of the totality of the disclosed material. We consider all those details when deciding on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I move now on to Rule 68(i) disclosure about exculpatory material. On the 13th of April, the Prosecution filed a motion seeking an extension of the general Rule 68(i) disclosure dead-line which was then set for the 30th of April, 2012. The Defence objected and irrespective of the Chamber's decision on the motion requested a 30-day adjournment of the start of the -- 90-day, yes, I misspoke, it is 90-day adjournment of the start of the trial. On the 26th of April, through an informal communication, the Chamber granted the Prosecution's motion for an extension for disclosure of Rule 68(i) materials in relation to the evidence it intends to lead after the summer recess. The dead-line of 30 April remained intact for the disclosure of Rule 68(i) materials which relate to evidence the Prosecution intends to lead before the summer recess. The Chamber denied, without prejudice, the Defence's request for an adjournment. Further, the Chamber instructed the Prosecution to file a notification in relation to Rule 68(i) materials related to evidence it intends to lead after the summer recess. And this decision is hereby put on the record. The Chamber would like to say a few words on disclosure generally. And, Mr. Lukic, this will perhaps clarify also the Chamber's denial, without prejudice, of your requests for adjournment of trial. And of course I'm talking about decisions we have given until now. We'll further consider the situation on the basis of the submissions you made five minutes ago. The Chamber's approach has been to set firm dead-lines for the completion of disclosure, rather than adopting an approach of rolling dead-lines throughout the trial. This approach has led the Chamber taking a more active and a more attentive role in pre-trial disclosure matters than has necessarily been the case in other trials in this Tribunal. It has also resulted in the vast majority of disclosure being completed during the pre-trial stage of the case. Notwithstanding this, the Chamber is aware that there may be disclosure of materials after the final deadlines have passed. This could include, for example, material that was not in the Prosecution's possession or did not even exist at the time of the dead-line. The Chamber considers that the consequences of any late disclosure should be determined by taking into account the scope of the problems, concrete problems, resulting from it. This means that the relevant factors are not only the amount of time between the dead-line for disclosure and the date when the material was actually disclosed. Additional factors include the reasons why the material was not disclosed earlier as well as the length, complexity, and importance of any non-disclosed documents. And further, what the appropriate remedy should be, if any remedy is necessary, that such remedy would depend on the specifics of the situation. For example, granting a temporary adjournment, postponing a specific witness's testimony, or ordering the re-call of a witness are all possible remedies for late disclosure depending on the circumstances. And I would want to leave it to that as a general observation by the Chamber on this matter. We, however, are still on the topic of Rule 68(i) disclosure. On the 1st of May, the Prosecution filed a notification on the status of the Rule 68(i) disclosure in relation to the evidence it intended to lead before the summer break. This report was also discussed at yesterday's 65 ter meeting. Mr. Groome, at the Rule 65 ter meeting you offered to provide an additional update on the status of Rule 68(i) disclosure. Are you in a position to do that now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm going to defer to my colleague, Mr. Bos, with respect to the latest information in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bos, may I invite you to update the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We spoke yesterday with the persons responsible for the review, and there are still two additional sheets that need to be reviewed. And at this stage it's not possible for us to give an exact number of the documents that still need to be reviewed, but it appears that we think that the review will be, at the latest, completed by the end of next week, so not at the end of this week but by the end of next week. But that's just for the review of the documents. And we still think that as far as finally disclosing all Rule 68 evidence, that we can still disclose all this material by the 8th of June. That dead-line would certainly not change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bos, could I ask you one thing. You are now using the term "sheet." When talking about the review yesterday we were talking about searches. I'm trying to understand where you said yesterday that 104 out of the 108 searches have been done, what exactly it means in terms of sheets or to what extent sheets are related to those searches?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, when I refer to a sheet, I refer to a search term, so it's -- it means two additional search terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So when you said 104 out of 108, we are now at 106 out of 108?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It sounds hesitant, Mr. Bos. Is there anything in your mind which makes you hesitate?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, the reason the two remaining ones are still to be processed, so it's -- at this stage it's unclear how many documents, in fact, need to be reviewed. The search results are coming from ISU and are then being looked at and reviewed by the reviewers to see how much of that material needs to be, in fact, reviewed. And that still needs to be done. So I can't give an exact figures on the numbers of documents to be reviewed, but we expect that the number will be such that we can finalise the complete review by the end of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then it will be further processed in order to make it ready for disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you say that will be complete by the 8th of June, but the review, so before the processing, will be complete by the end of next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this update. Mr. Lukic, any further questions in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Since this dead-line is self-imposed by the Prosecution, we have nothing to add on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Groome, the Chamber has already explained that it will determine the consequences of any late disclosure of materials by taking into consideration the scope of the problems resulting from this late disclosure. However, the Chamber also wishes to clarify that it did not grant a dead-line extension for Rule 68(i) materials in relation to evidence that the Prosecution intends to lead before the summer recess. The Chamber would, as a practical matter, strongly encourage the Prosecution to prioritise the review, processing and disclosure, so I'm talking about the whole of the process, of any residual material in relation to evidence potentially relevant to the first stage of the trial. Further, the Prosecution should look for ways, if possible, to disclose these materials on hard disk to the Defence at the earliest possible moment, perhaps by reconsidering some of the pre-disclosure steps which are relevant to EDS organising, but not the disclosure on hard disk -- not relevant for the disclosure on hard disks. These are not instructions from the Chamber, Mr. Groome. They are merely practical considerations that we encourage you to keep in mind. And this will be further addressed later today in relation to the Prosecution's witness order list for its first 23 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will certainly give that consideration, but I do want to assure the Chamber that from January of 2012, Mr. Brammertz has made the disclosure in this case the absolute top priority and that all available resources have been devoted to it and many steps have been taken to try to do it in the most efficient and quickest way possible. So it has had the top priority now for the past four months, but of course we will endeavour to - as we always do - re-examine our work to see are we doing it as quickly and efficiently as possible. As I pointed out to the Chamber yesterday, that it may be possible to simply take all of this material and put it in image files, just picture files, onto a hard drive, but I think that's of limited utility to the Defence. But if the Chamber instructs or if Mr. Lukic requests, we can simply take all of that material and put it in its current state which is picture files, unsearchable, and provide that, I would think, more quickly. Although as I said yesterday, that process itself would require staff which would then be taken from the process of making it searchable and making it in a way that is usable by the Defence. But we will certainly take the Chamber's comments just now under serious consideration, and if there are ways that we can improve or further prioritise, we will certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course the Chamber - also I think I said that yesterday as well - the Chamber encourages the parties to see what is possible but also what is needed by the Defence. And to the extent that Mr. Lukic would be more happy to already receive some material or if only the description of the materials that are further processed, one line, order, date this and this, issued by that and that and that, even before it is further processed and even before -- and not perhaps even having received the not-searchable document, that at least he knows what documents are at that moment processed. If he would wish to receive that information, I think you should seriously consider that. If he, however, says no, let's wait until we have received the fully processed material, I'll not look at it on the basis of just description of the document, then of course I can imagine that you would not spend more resources on doing this intermediate step. Again, I clearly said that the Chamber is not giving instructions but is urging the parties to seek to proceed in such a way that Mr. Lukic receives materials as soon as possible even if it's not yet in the perfect stage if he considers it's important to have that available. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you for assisting us on this issue. I said we have no problem with 8th of June for this disclosure. When I said that I was having in mind that the trial will not start in May, because of course we cannot cross-examine any witness without having materials that can go against the witness who is testifying against Mr. Mladic. So if we want to be prepared, of course we have to have 68 -- Rule 68(i) materials before any witness appears here for testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, as you may be well aware, we do not know what the result of these searches and reviews will be, so therefore it may well be that it doesn't affect in any way, well, let's say, witness number 2 or witness number 5, or 1 to 5. We do not know yet. And as I explained earlier, the Chamber is considering the problems resulting from late disclosure which could be, as I said before, re-calling a witness in order to fully exercise the right to confront the witness also with the material which you had not received then. And of course, neither the Chamber nor the Prosecution nor the Defence is seeking such a situation to arise. But as I said before, we'll consider it in the way I set out 15 or 20 minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just simply to say that after speaking with Ms. Stewart, it would be possible for the Prosecution to provide the disclosure sheets of the raw data that -- pre-reviewed. This would have the ERN numbers of the documents that were identified by the search terms alone before any review was done. Many of the documents identified may already be on the general collection of the EDS. The descriptions, however, are flawed. One of the things that we do is to improve those descriptions in those sheets as part of the processing process. But we would be willing to provide that to Mr. Lukic as soon as possible if he thought that would assist his work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would not take great efforts to produce that? That's relatively easily done?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart advised me that that particular assistance would be fairly easy to do and would not set back the overall project.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And at the same time would at least give Mr. Lukic a first impression in what he could expect as a result of --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not exactly, Your Honour, because in the review process it would be a much smaller list. Many of those documents would not be potentially exculpatory. They would simply be documents that had the particular search term that was run across our collection of 9 million documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it may assist you, it may not assist you. It's relatively easily produced. I take it that you will then receive that soon, which allows you perhaps not exactly what you wanted to do, but at least gives some possibilities of looking at the material which may finally result from the Rule 68 review of the large number of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I move on. Mr. Lukic, in the Prosecution's notification, the Prosecution states that an additional disclosure was made to the Defence on the 1st of May. And at the Rule 65 ter meeting you confirmed the receipt of the hard disk but you also stated that you have not yet gone through them. Are you in a position to confirm that the correct materials were disclosed to you yesterday or are you not yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I did have time to see in general what's disclosed on these three -- actually two DVDs and one CD. On the CD we had only spreadsheet. It is, if I'm not wrong, only 68(i) material, so it has nothing to do with 66 and 65 materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think we are at this moment talking about 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 68, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that material was in relation to Kljuc and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Prijedor, yes. So at least for those municipalities then you have -- you have received that Rule 68(i) material.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But I have -- I just want to point out that the first witness is in connection with Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, for example, we don't have anything for the first municipality that would appear here in front of Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And any Prosecution response to that or any other matter to be raised in this context?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to be more precise. With respect to the first witness, the Prosecution has fully disclosed the results of its searches with respect to any information in our system that could affect the credibility of that witness. What has not been processed is general substantive material related to Kotor Varos in general, not even necessarily related to the specific crime which this witness -- this witness gives rather limited evidence about a very particular crime. So it's not even that. It's just general potentially exculpatory material about events generally in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you would say if the scope of the testimony of the witness is very limited, that whatever would touch upon that testimony, any exculpatory material is disclosed, but that might not be true for the whole of the Kotor Varos environment, to say so. That's other things not directly related to the testimony of the witness which may have happened in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And it's the Prosecution's firm belief that it is an extremely low probability that the searches that still remain to be done, to be completed, would generate any material that was potentially exculpatory to the -- either the witness himself or to the substance of his testimony. The Prosecution's position would be that the more appropriate course of action, since we've already made travel plans for this witness and he comes from a country quite far away, that if the Chamber or Mr. Lukic should believe that some material disclosed late would have been useful during the cross-examination, that the more prudent course would be to simply re-call the witness at a later time. That would be our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. We discussed it to some extent, although not the last portion, during yesterday's 65 ter meeting. Anything you would like to add, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I would like to move on to the 65 ter exhibit list upload in e-court. On the 26th of April, the Prosecution informed the Chamber that all Rule 65 ter exhibits had been successfully uploaded into e-court, with the exception of some residual errors which meant that it had failed to upload certain exhibits. In a filing of the 1st of May, the Defence confirmed that the Rule 65 ter exhibits were available to it as of the evening of the 26th of April. At yesterday's Rule 65 ter meeting, Mr. Groome, you clarified that a sizeable error list remains and offered to provide a further update today. And I'd like to invite you to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only additional information that I have that's different from yesterday, yesterday I informed the Chamber that we had devoted staff to make a special effort to upload all of the exhibits that were likely to be used with the first 23 witnesses, and that as of yesterday we had accomplished that with 13. We will now have completed all of the witnesses by -- just one second, Your Honour. We will have completed that with respect to all of the 23 witnesses by the end of tomorrow. So by the end of tomorrow, all of the exhibits that will be used prior to the summer break will be uploaded, the problem sorted out, and available on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since the upload is not fully complete, although complete for the first 23 witnesses, the Chamber would instruct the Prosecution to continue to update the Chamber on a weekly basis by -- through an informal communication by e-mail until the upload is complete and the updates should include the resolution of all the residual errors.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then finally, at the 65 ter meeting, the Prosecution was instructed to file a response to the Defence's 1st of May filing, particularly in relation to the timing and the status of disclosure to the Defence in relation to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter documents. And that instruction already given is hereby put on the record. I now move to Rule 70 providers. Mr. Groome, do you have an update in relation to disclosure of the diary which we discussed yesterday at the Rule 65 ter meeting or an update on any other Rule 70 matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With respect to the diary, Mr. McCloskey will address the Chamber on that. And I think it's probably perhaps more appropriate that we go into private session for the discussion of that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. And I'll move to the next item on my agenda, which deals with the witness order list. At last week's Pre-Trial Conference, the Chamber instructed the Prosecution to file by the 2nd of May an amended list setting out the witness order for the witnesses to be called to testify until the summer recess. At yesterday's Rule 65 ter meeting, the Chamber instructed the Prosecution not to file this list until receiving further instructions from the Chamber. In addition to the Chamber's Rule 73 bis (C) decision and other decisions announced last week -- at last week's Pre-Trial Conference, Mr. Groome, the Chamber expects the Prosecution to take into account the relevant disclosure developments since last week. For example, the Prosecution could consider calling first those witnesses unaffected by the Rule 66(A)(ii) batch 5 errors. The Prosecution could also consider whether it is feasible to schedule for a later time in the first stage of the trial those witnesses for whom there might be residual Rule 68(i) materials not yet disclosed. In this respect I refer you to your 1st of May filing, paragraphs 7 and 8 specifically. utterances.text: Then we would like to hear from you as soon as possible whether you oppose any of the five additional -- added categories which all very much look as if they are not serving any direct forensic purpose in this case. But we would first like to hear from you. Then presentation and tendering of evidence is next on my list. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'm done with my items on the agenda. Mr. Groome, yesterday you indicated that you would like to have approximately 20 minutes to make a submission in relation to the Chamber's guidance on the presentation and the tendering of evidence. The Chamber has considered this request and grants you the requested 20 minutes. Therefore, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It may assist the Chamber to have an enumeration of the guide-lines as the Prosecution understands them. I've given copies to the Court Officer and ask that they be handed up now and I've given Mr. Lukic a copy prior to sitting today. And I'd also would just please inform our interpreters that I have provided copies of the written text of this to them. Hopefully that will assist them in their work. Your Honours, thank you for giving me time to address you on the issue of the guide-lines. They are a matter of great concern for the Prosecution. The four primary reasons they are of concern are the following. The guide-lines force the Prosecution to use court time unnecessarily and is therefore inefficient. The Prosecution has been given a limited amount of court time, 200 hours, in which to present its evidence, an admittedly large volume of evidence. Based on the prior practice of the Tribunal, we carefully developed a case we could present in 200 hours. The guide-lines would significantly impact the proceedings by calling into question our ability to meet our high burden of proof at trial in that limited amount of time. Two, the guide-lines make large categories of evidence it has collected and adduced over the years presumptively inadmissible. Despite the fact that the very same evidence has been admitted and accepted by other Chambers, going out to obtain new statements which meet the particular specifications of the guide-lines results in an unnecessary and enormous expenditure of resources and time. Three, the guide-lines force the Prosecution to take new statements of witnesses despite the fact that these witnesses have already provided sworn evidence that is admissible under the Rules. Forcing the Prosecution to get new statements will delay the trial because we will need time to do that. The statements will have to be translated and they are, of course, disclosable material. The process of taking new statements will be a hardship to witnesses and in some cases be a re-traumatisation of those witnesses. Fourth, the guide-lines encroach upon the independence of the Prosecutor as established in Article 16 of the Statute. It does this by creating new criteria for admissibility - criteria not found in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence with respect to the evidence the Prosecution can tender. The Prosecution has the obligation and the right to investigate, collect, and present the evidence supporting the indictment. The guide-line places unnecessary, presumptive, and arbitrary restrictions on the Prosecution's ability to present its case and impede its ability to do so efficiently. At the outset I want to say that the Prosecution recognises that the guide-lines are an attempt to develop a more efficient trial procedure that fully guarantees a fair process for Mr. Mladic. The Prosecution commends the Chamber for this effort. The Prosecution considers that it has an independent obligation to prosecute its case in a fair and efficient manner and has -- and will in the future do everything to further this obligation. The Prosecution has already demonstrated its commitment to this principle in this particular case. The Prosecution requests the following: That the guide-lines as promulgated to date be considered a clear expression of the Chamber's preferences with respect to the evidence presented before the Chamber, preferences that, wherever possible, the Prosecution will seek to abide by, and that any presumptive limitation on the type of evidence the Prosecution can tender, the time the Prosecution can use to examine a 92 ter witness, the number of exhibits that can be tendered with a particular witness be abandoned and that such determinations be made on a case-by-case basis by the Trial Chamber in its application of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I would like to present you with a few examples of the impact of the guide-lines. I will first address guide-line 2, the Chamber's presumptive bar on the introduction of prior witness testimony pursuant to Rules 92 bis and ter. Guide-line 2 would force the Prosecution to expend enormous resources, personnel and financial, in taking new statements which would be less reliable than a witness's prior cross-examined evidence. In many cases those new statements would re-traumatise victim witnesses. In other cases, witnesses are adverse to the Prosecution and would be unlikely to co-operate with the Prosecution and provide statements. In November 1994, Dzenana Sokolovic was shot while crossing a Sarajevo street with her 7-year-old son Nermin. The bullet passed through her abdomen and struck Nermin in the head, killing him instantly. A member of my staff met with her last week. She found Ms. Sokolovic to still suffer very deeply the effects of that day. Discussing the event was extremely difficult. The Prosecution considers that an appropriate exercise of its discretion would be to adduce her evidence via 92 bis. Her original statement did not include all of the essential information. She gave testimony in the Dragomir Milosevic case, a complete account of the event occupies approximately 45 pages of transcript. Indeed, as Ms. Sokolovic does not provide evidence relevant to the acts and conduct of the accused, the Chamber's guide-line suggest that the Chamber too would prefer her evidence to be adduced via 92 bis. The Prosecution has the right under Rule 92 bis to tender her prior testimony. Guide-line number 2 prevents it from doing so and forces us to either call her viva voce or to take a new ICTY statement. Either way, Ms. Sokolovic would suffer more because of what happened 18 years ago. Forcing the Prosecution to get new statements will delay the trial because we will need time to arrange to go on missions, to meet witnesses, redraft statements, have witnesses review and make changes and finalise the statements. In some 92 bis cases the witness will need to sign a new declaration. This will be a drain also on Registry resources. The statements will then have to be translated and disclosed. As a matter of law, her cross-examined testimony given over five years ago, closer to the time of the event, would be entitled to more weight than any new statement we would take today. The guide-lines effectively force the Prosecution to take its best evidence of Nermin's death and simply not use it, not use it and instead take a new statement that is likely to be less reliable and cause significant hardship to the witness. RM070 was a brave woman who gave public testimony of her repeated rapes by Bosnian Serb soldiers in another trial. Only her identity was concealed. She did this so the Tribunal would have in its records a public account of what so many women suffered. Guide-line number 2 puts the Prosecution in the position of being unable to use this courageous and cross-examined evidence and to lead her evidence once again in its entirety or to go and try to reduce her testimony into a written statement. This would require substantial time and would undoubtedly re-traumatise her. There are a significant number of Prosecution witnesses who are considered or properly considered adverse witnesses for which the Prosecution intends to tender their cross-examined testimony. The Prosecution is not in possession of witness statements and it is unlikely to be able to get such statements. Consider the case of RM349. The Prosecution has no ICTY statement from RM349, a witness who has given evidence in both the Popovic and Tolimir cases. He is currently working as an investigator on a Defence team for another related case before this Tribunal. His testimony in the Tolimir case given last year is the best evidence now in possession of the Prosecution. The guide-lines prohibit its use. We anticipate that he would be reluctant to give a statement. Ljubomir Obradovic, the Prosecution has no statement. There is a transcript that can be tendered. It has been accepted in other cases, lastly by the Karadzic Trial Chamber. This Chamber has promulgated guide-lines never encountered in any of the trials to date before this Tribunal. The very evidence admitted before other Chambers is now presumptively inadmissible before this Trial Chamber. There are 29 witnesses in the Srebrenica component of the case alone for which there is no statement, witnesses who are properly considered adverse to the Prosecution, witnesses who are unlikely to willingly participate in the taking of a statement. Your Honours, we accept your preference for statements and where we have them and can appropriately use them, we will. But the first guide-line, the requirement that 92 bis and ter motions are limited to a single consolidated statement, impedes our ability to do so. Last week the Chamber relaxed this guide-line to some degree with 92 bis witnesses and said it would contemplate the introduction of a short supplemental statement. Even in the case of 92 bis witnesses, in a significant number of cases the Prosecution has two substantive statements, each dealing with a separate significant body of evidence. Consider witness RM274, a protected witness who provided evidence in the Tolimir and Karadzic Chambers. The witness has two significant statements. He is suffering from PTSD. He says he does not want to hear from us again but we are free to use his statements. The guide-lines require us to go to that witness and consolidate the two statements. We reasonably anticipate that he will not co-operate. We reasonably anticipate that approaching him will aggravate his PTSD. We face a similar situation with RM358. There are 11 witnesses in the Srebrenica component of the case alone whose evidence now resides in two substantive statements. With respect to no supplemental statements for 92 ter witnesses, Judge Orie, in the Stanisic and Simatovic case you established a practice where the Prosecution and the Defence in the case of 92 ter witnesses were permitted to have witnesses create a chart of all of the amendments the witness requested to make to their original statement or testimony. For witnesses with many corrections, this process saved a significant amount of time. We understand the guide-lines to now prevent the Prosecution from doing this and require each of these corrections to be led live in court. I submit an inefficient use of time. Guide-line 4 presumptively limits the number of exhibits a witness can give evidence about in a written statement to five. Guide-line 5 prohibits the tendering of any associated exhibits with 92 ter witnesses. Each of the exhibits must be adduced live in court. Looking at specific witnesses shows that the implementation of this rule would result in an unnecessary use of court time. First, I'd like to point to the -- in the case of 92 bis witnesses. Dr. Youssef Hajir was a doctor who worked in Sarajevo during the siege. He provides evidence of the treatment of victims of one sniping and two shelling incidents. The Prosecution seeks to tender his evidence via 92 bis. His evidence includes more than five exhibits, the medical records of victims of the crimes in this indictment. The guide-lines force the Prosecution to exceptionally justify the tendering of more than five exhibits. There is no exceptional justification other than the fact that the exhibits are directly relevant to an adjudication of this indictment. In the alternative, the guide-lines would require us to call him to testify here in court and tender the exhibits live in court, to essentially have him read information on documents that the Chamber is well able to read itself, an unnecessary expenditure of time. Similarly, RM055 is an international observer in Sarajevo and was present during the second Markale shelling. The Prosecution intends to adduce this evidence via 92 bis. According to the law of his country, his statement needed to be taken in a somewhat involved judicial process. That process has been completed. There are approximately 12 documents associated with that statement, exhibits which include multiple letters of protest to Mladic and other senior VRS officers. A 92 bis witness by the name of Stephanie Frease provides important evidence regarding intercepted communications, again more than five exhibits. One of the detrimental impacts of the guide-lines would be that it would prior the Prosecution to devote much of the time for its case presentation to the introduction of documents through witnesses with no direct knowledge of the crimes. It would be unfortunate and possibly misunderstood by members of the public to view this last trial about the crimes in Bosnia and see little or no victims and primarily people who kept records. With respect to 92 ter, David Harland is an example of how the fifth guide-line impacts on 92 ter witnesses. He was a senior UN official present in Bosnia for most of the war. He participated in numerous high-level meetings with Mladic, Karadzic, and others. The Prosecution intends to tender his amalgamated statement, a statement which has as associated exhibits his contemporaneous meeting notes and situation reports. His statement gives necessary context to these documents and the Chamber can read the meeting reports for itself to have the best evidence of what happened in those meetings. Guide-line 5 prohibits the Prosecution from tendering the associated exhibits, despite them meeting the clear legal standard of the Tribunal's jurisprudence and it forces us to unnecessarily use hearing time to adduce this evidence. Similarly, Dr. Bakir Nakas treated victims of 14 different crimes in Sarajevo. The Prosecution estimates that it can lead his evidence 92 ter with the necessary and only the necessary medical records in about 30 minutes. An approach adopted by the Perisic Trial Chamber with this witness, an approach adopted by the Karadzic Trial Chamber with this witness, an approach now rejected by this Trial Chamber. The guide-lines require the Prosecution to have Dr. Nakas discuss each document live in court, a process that would require several hours of direct evidence, not the 30 minutes that this process can take using the Rules appropriately. The same issues apply to many other witnesses. I'll simply note the case of Momir Nikolic. He has approximately 20 exhibits as part of his 92 ter package, each one of them important for the Chamber to have before it. The guide-lines would force the Prosecution to lead the evidence of these 20 documents, adding significant time to an already lengthy examination. Finally, Your Honours, guide-line 6 restricts the examination of 92 ter witnesses to 30 minutes. The guide-line prohibits the Prosecution from using perhaps the most effective tool for achieving real efficiency in the trial. It can be used with witnesses who have an abundance of substantive and directly relevant evidence. When used appropriately, the Prosecution can introduce a great deal of evidence in written form and use a focused, direct examination to lead evidence of particular relevant in this case that is not dealt with in the prior statement or testimony. For example, again the case of Momir Nikolic. His direct examination in the Tolimir case took nine hours and 20 minutes, in the Karadzic case it took six hours. We believe that if the Chamber allows us to tender his evidence using in part the tool of 92 ter, we can deal with matters of particular significance to this case in a two-hour direct examination, a savings of four to seven hours of court time with a single witness. Guide-line 6 presumptively makes this impossible and forces the Prosecution to call Nikolic and many, many other witnesses viva voce in order to adduce the evidence necessary to meet our burden of proof, evidence that would be impossible to lead in 30 minutes. Your Honours, we developed a case that we could present in 200 hours based on the prior developed practices of this Tribunal. The guide-lines make it impossible to adduce all of the evidence necessary to meet our burden of proof in 200 hours. To the extent that the Chamber would not allot us any additional time, the guide-lines serve to improperly and unfairly impede the Prosecution's ability to present its case. Your Honours, I recognise that you have said that you will deviate from the guide-lines in exceptional circumstances. Last week when I asked for clarification about what this new legal standard for admissibility - the exceptional circumstances - would be, the Chamber informed us: "We'll first all consider to what extent it is possible to identify exactly what exceptional circumstances are because it's a rather abstract term, and if we think we are able to do so, we will give you further guidance." Your Honours, it would be irresponsible for us as Prosecutors to proceed in the presentation of the Prosecution case not knowing what this test would be. To do so we could be proceeding with the uncertainty of whether we will be able to meet this undefined standard and, hence, meet our burden of proof in the time currently allotted for the case. Your Honours, in conclusion, all the Prosecution asks is that you amend the legal effect of the guide-lines so that they are understood to be an expression of the strong preference of the Chamber, a preference we will seek to abide by wherever we can appropriately do so. I ask that the presumptive and arbitrary exclusions of evidence or restrictions of evidence that can only be overcome by exceptional circumstances be completely abandoned and replaced with a carefully considered and reasoned approach to the presentation of evidence and the particular circumstances of individual witnesses. Judge Orie, I make my last submission with some reluctance because it is not my intention to embarrass you, but it is something that must be said. You have presided over the only case that I am aware of in the entire history of the Tribunal in which a significant and demonstrable and measurable level of efficiency was achieved. Your administration of that trial and that Trial Chamber's willingness to consider time-saving methods of adducing proof --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I'm going to interrupt you here, the guide-lines, the guidance comes from the Chamber and what happened in another case was decided by that Chamber. Therefore, I think that - but let me consider that further with my colleagues in a second - I think it's inappropriate to address individual Judges on this kind of matters. But before I take this position as a firm position of this Chamber, I would have to consult with my colleagues. It underlines how much I am aware that I'm functioning in a collegial system.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I accept that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, the Chamber has no problem whatsoever if you refer to practices which were -- which you have seen in other cases, but that should be irrespective of whether Judges in those cases are sitting in this case or not, let alone that you personally address Judges for that purpose. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was not my purpose and I apologise. I did not mean to draw undue attention to you as an individual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you did so rather explicitly. You even apologised for it -- for that. I think the apologies were the better part of your submission. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did it only to point out that in that particular case, the Prosecution was able to adduce its case in less than -- in half the time that it originally estimated and a third less time than the Trial Chamber had estimated and it had allotted for that case. I simply raise that to strongly urge this Chamber not to abandon practices that have worked in other trials in favour of presumptive guide-lines that are clearly going to create significant delays and inefficiencies in this trial process, delays that are entirely unnecessary and avoidable. I thank you for receiving my submissions today and for your consideration of the matter which is of paramount importance to the Prosecution. Should you reject this application, I would respectfully ask that the Chamber do so in a reasoned written opinion so that the Prosecutor can more carefully consider how best to proceed. I am prepared now to address any particular questions or concerns that the Chamber may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Lukic, is there anything you would like to say in response? Because we have a few matters. First of all, the Chamber will consider whether we will just consider the matter on the basis of this oral submission or whether we would invite the Prosecution to make a written submission on the matter. We will first have to discuss that further. Mr. Lukic, I do not know whether you would want to reserve your right to respond to this submission or whether you would already like to respond now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just like to respond briefly, Your Honour, orally, and if necessary we can respond to their -- to the Prosecution's written submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks. We are always in the same position even in our local jurisdictions. The Prosecution is always aware of efficiency and the Defence is always more aware of protection of human rights and of having a fair trial for the defendant. Even before we responded to requests made by the Prosecution to change your guide-lines, and every time we emphasize that we are happy with the guide-lines we received from the Chamber. So we just reiterate this position now. When my learned friend talked about 92 bis statements and their intention to introduce transcripts, it is very hard to believe that there is no anything substantial in the transcript that goes against the Rule 92 bis, and Defence will object any written statement tendered under the Rule 92 bis if it goes to prove that the acts and conduct of the accused as charged in the indictment because it is directly against the rule, and this also goes to the acts and conduct of subordinates of the accused. So we think that any transcript is not good tool to have 92 bis statement introduced for any witness. And when discussed about the exhibits, the limitation of five exhibits per the witness, and if you decide to deviate from your first decision, then it would be -- impact the time allocated to the Defence to cross-examine the witness. So the whole system of the guide-lines has to be changed. That's all we had at this time, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, of course we'll consider your submissions, which are relatively large. I would, first of all, have a brief question to Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic, I would have a short question for you. If I understood you well, but I'll re-read, you say acts and conduct of the accused is a bar to admission under Rule 92 bis. But there -- it would include -- let me just find it, one second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 92 bis says: "... to proof of a matter other than the acts and conduct of the accused as charged in the indictment."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What I was -- you were talking about the subordinates. Do you have -- yes, I'm -- well, I think I'm at page 46, line 20. Do you have case law to say that whatever is done by subordinates is excluded and is included in acts and conduct as charged against the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know it by heart. We addressed it before. But I can tell you that according to the indictment, every single military person, police officer, and even local Serbs according to the indictment are subordinate to my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But are there other cases where whatever someone who was subordinated was -- or under the -- whether that was all excluded. We'll have a look at it but that is, of course, one of the issues we'll have to specifically research in order to follow your rather general rejection of almost of the 92 bis material.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry that I have to disappoint you, but I really don't know by heart the case law of the Tribunal. I can address it in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not blaming you for that. Mr. Groome, you gave a lot of examples. We'll have to consider it on a more abstract level as well, although I know that it's a dangerous expression at this moment in view of what you just said. For example, you gave the example of Dr. Youssef Hajir. Now, I don't have his statement anywhere on my mind, but I can imagine that if a doctor and if he testified in the Galic case, which I don't know whether he did or not, but I've seen similar evidence, then you get sometimes a statement where a doctor says I treated this person and we did that and that, it was on that and that day, et cetera, et cetera, and then you find a long list of medical documentation attached to that. Is it your understanding that without the medical documentation, you would not accept if a doctor says he was brought in on that same day, we found that the person had bullet wounds, we treated him, et cetera, et cetera. Of course the medical documentation would tell us exactly what kind of antibiotics he was administered or -- well, whatever, or whether the person died and we have then a report. I mean, to what extent do you think that such evidence would not be convincing without those documents? Of course it can be challenged. Of course if the other party comes and says, well, we don't believe the doctor, the other party knowing that all this medical documentation exists will think it over twice before it starts challenging it, because then we would be in a situation where, of course, I take it, the Prosecution would provide that medical documentation and not just rely on what the doctor said. I'm -- I was just wondering what your thoughts are, and I take one of the examples. Again, I'm not addressing at this moment, and certainly not on behalf of the Chamber, the merits of your submissions. But I just wondered how you look at this in view of my question of such a statement by a doctor on a specific date mentioning specific persons. Why -- what the medical documentation adds until there is a challenge to that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I recognise the importance of your point, and if the Chamber reviews our filings on the 10th of February with respect to our witness list, the Prosecution there said that it was our understanding that none of the elements of the crimes here, the severity of the injury, was something that needed to be established. And the Prosecution in that filing indicated that we would not be producing large amounts of medical documentation unless there was a challenge. Having said that, in a sniping case it may be very, very important for the Chamber to see the original intake sheet where the body of the victim is indicated and there's a line going through the -- showing the entry wound and the exit wound. And it is the Prosecution's case where there is a medical record that is directly relevant to the Chamber's adjudication of that particular crime, that is something the Chamber should have before it. And we would not be seeking to tender every exhibit tendered in prior evidence that a witness may have given. And if the Chamber reviews the filings that we have made to date, we have substantially reduced the number of filings. In the filing for Osman S elak we reduced it from about 80 documents to about 41 documents. So we are trying to go through the documents that are associated exhibits and really limit them to only that which is essential for this Chamber's determination of this indictment. I take the Chamber's point and it is something that we do intend to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, for example, if I look at your example you're talking about treating of victims of one sniping and two shelling incidents. Now, first of all, I have no idea whether these are five victims from shelling incidents or not. What the experience has taught us over the years is that often those who were victims of shelling incidents had injuries or died as a result from shrapnel, whereas, as you, I think, rightly point out, for sniping victims it may be specifically relevant, which already raises the question here whether you could make a distinction between attaching or using associated exhibits specifically on sniping. And then for sniping I would be inclined to agree with you that sometimes the details of the wounds are very important, sometimes they are not. So therefore, that's -- this is the kind of thoughts that come to my mind if I hear you say that a doctor who gave a statement on the treatment of victims of sniping and shelling incidents, that to what extent, if not challenged, if the statement is not challenged, because if, of course, the Defence would say this doctor was -- was not working in that hospital but then we have a different challenge or the doctor must have invented all of this because -- then, of course, you would rely on any medical documentation which I would say in the first round you may well do without or with only a small portion of it. These are the thoughts that came to my mind and that's the reason why I asked you how you look at such an example if I give a different angle of view on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I fully agree with that. It is our intention that prior to the submission of any 92 ter or 92 bis application, to do a very careful review to make sure that only essential evidence is being put before the Chamber. I would discourage any blanket rules that it's necessary for sniping but not for shelling --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- because I can imagine a case where the shrapnel is recovered and it identifies the weapon used. But I assure the Chamber that that is our intention, and if it assists the Chamber, the Prosecution would be prepared in its 92 bis and ter submissions to set out why we believe the particular exhibit that we want to tender as an associated exhibit is directly relevant to the adjudication in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, not only relevant, but necessary for the appreciation of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's a different standard, you see. Let me -- I have no further questions. We'll have to consider your submissions, Mr. Groome. You spent quite some time on it. This is not to blame you for that, but it takes us adequate time as well to consider it. And it will -- the result of our further consideration of the matters you brought to our attention, of course, will be important for how to proceed, whether you'd like to further make further submissions or whether you would seek a decision from the Chamber on the matter. So let's first think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then is there any other matter any of the parties would like to raise at this moment? If not ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, I think we are still waiting for the matter you would like to raise in relation to the use of technical facilities in the Detention Unit if I understood you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. First of all, we hope that we will cure some of problems Mr. Mladic has with EDS system by disclosing him those batches of witnesses we received from the Prosecution recently. Otherwise, for him it's almost useless to use this room since he can do it only twice a week, I think two hours a day. So it's four hours in total per week. So it's not of much use. And he is not able to use these facilities yet since nobody provided him with the proper training and with the translation of the manuals so he could at least follow every time the proceeding, how to log on, and so on. So that system is not working for him at this moment at all, although we are thankful for -- to the Chamber for helping us to have this system introduced at the first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does this mean - sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Lukic - that Mr. Mladic has received no training at all? That's not, I think, what was relayed to the Chamber. And if there's a concern about that, then, of course, we would have to further inquire into what support Mr. Mladic has received, how he has tried to use the facilities --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He did -- sorry. He did receive some training, but due to his problems with short-term memory, he needs that manual every time to log on and it's in English, and when he's sitting there alone with English manual, he's not able to manipulate the computer and the system at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I didn't have the details on my mind, but my staff reminds me that we received on the 23rd of April a message from the Registry that on the 19th of April, that Mr. Mladic had been provided with at least some B/C/S manual material which would assist him. Now, I'm -- this seems to contradict what you are saying. Certainly a reason to further verify. Have you verified it or is it just on the basis of what Mr. Mladic told you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think it would be wise if you get in touch with those who are assisting Mr. Mladic in this respect and find out whether it is true that there's no B/C/S manual been given, and if that would be the case, then of course we would further verify on what basis we have received the information we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just saw English manual in his hands the last time I visit Mr. Mladic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- so it's the only thing I could verify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think it would be good before this matter is raised that you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I am informed by the Registry of the following. The following confirmation of receipt: "I, the undersigned, Ratko Mladic, confirm that I've been issued with the following: EDS manual in B/C/S." And this was signed on the 19th of April and it's signed -- it appears that Mr. Mladic's signature is on this document. So therefore I think before raising this matter in court, perhaps try to find the B/C/S manual. I would be surprised if despite this signed receipt that Mr. Mladic would not have it somewhere. Again if another copy is needed or if lost it, then we should, of course, try to resolve such problems. But it seems that the basis for this part of your submission is not very strong at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I feel much as a hearsay witness, Your Honour, because -- that's why I prepared -- [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Lukic, and therefore perhaps it would be good to verify these matters before you raise them in court, but no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Mladic asked me if it is possible to give him a couple of minutes so he has to address some also technical things from the UNDU and I would rather not interfere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course we are not in a Status Conference here. I will first discuss matters, whether this is appropriately done in this way or whether we would invite you to make a submission, a written submission on the matter, or a submission on behalf of Mr. Mladic orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just first consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber considers it appropriate if you raise the matters and not Mr. Mladic. And of course this is not -- it -- this decision is also based on previous experiences and strictly keeping to the subject matter to be raised. So please raise the matter Mr. Mladic would like to have raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He just wants to raise some problems with the visits from family and friends and also some -- his written communication with friends and family, some letters were returned to him. So I'm afraid I don't know all the details and I could be wrong again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, first of all, you will understand that these are matters - however important they may be at this moment for Mr. Mladic - are not typically subject for a Pre-Trial Conference. So therefore, I would encourage Mr. Mladic to communicate with you and that you, first of all, try to resolve these matters, visit matters, with the UNDU and with the Registry. The same would be true for the correspondence, whatever matters there are. If they finally would have an impact on the proceedings and the fairness of the proceedings, you know that they can be raised before the Chamber. But of course, we would not deal with the matter unless it has first of all been appropriately dealt with and that you would have addressed the competent authorities for visits, for et cetera, that is, the Registry. So therefore I think that we should not deal with them at this moment in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then any other matter to be raised by the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then how are we going to proceed? Because we are at the conclusion --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of this Pre-Trial Conference. Mr. Lukic, the Chamber has considered how it would consider your request for a delay in the start of the trial for 90 days. We have discussed it during the last break, but we'll -- we don't want to hurry ourselves. We'll take our time to consider, especially perhaps also re-read your submissions of this morning. Nevertheless, it's also an urgent matter, we can't wait long. The Chamber hopes to be able to reach a decision today and communicate it to the parties already in an informal way, but to give reasons for it at a later moment in writing, whether that would be a written decision or whether it would be reasons given for a decision which would be put on the record orally earlier. We do not know yet. But we really try to -- we really hope to be able to tell the parties today whether or not we would grant the delay as you requested. Mr. Groome, that helps you out for the filing of tomorrow if we would be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If not, then at least we would do it as quickly as we can. So as matters --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask would it be possible for the Chamber to adjust its dead-line for the submission of the amended witness list to 24 hours after we receive the decision of the Chamber? Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it will be 24 hours after the Chamber has communicated its decision on the request of Mr. Lukic for a delay in the start of the trial of 90 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore with, of course, this reservation on our mind, as matters stand now - and that's how we'll proceed at this moment - we -- the opening statement of the Prosecution is scheduled and will begin on the 16th of May and most likely continue on the 17th of May. We therefore, as matters stand now, adjourn until the 16th of May, courtroom and exact time to be announced by the Registry at a later date. We stand adjourned.
